newsitem.title: USA: Airline costs for Boeing 737 changes to be minimal.
newsitem.headline: Airline costs for Boeing 737 changes to be minimal.

text.p: U.S. airlines would face miminal costs to comply with a call for safety changes in Boeing 737 aircraft, analysts said.
U.S. safety officials have recommended sweeping changes in the "rudder and yaw" control systems of the Boeing 737 to avoid sudden and uncontrolled rolls.
Those proposals, which follow a series of unexplained 737 crashes, including a 1994 USAir crash near Pittsburgh, have not yet been mandated by the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration.
"I don't expect it to have a big impact" for airlines, said Jeffrey Long, an analyst with J.P. Morgan.

"Airlines face 'airworthiness directives' all the time. These things are built into ongoing maintenance budgets," Long said. "This directive was just one that happened to make the newspapers. I'm underwhelmed by it. I suspect minimal impact," said Steve Lewins, an airline analyst with Gruntal & Co.

Analysts said airlines, not the manufacturers, typically bear the costs for required changes. Boeing Co did not immediately respond to requests for comment on whether or not it would be responsible for any costs.
Lehman Brothers' Brian Harris said Southwest Airlines Co and USAir Group Inc would have the greatest exposure to possible costs.
Southwest's entire fleet is comprised of 737s, while the aircraft dominate about 52.5 percent of USAir's, Harris said.
Continental Airlines Inc, UAL Corp's United Airlines and Delta Air Lines Inc would also face additional maintenance costs if the changes were mandated, Harris said.
USAir spokesman Paul Turk said it has already initiated some of the safety proposals, such as adding new pilot training.
USAir declined to comment on potential costs of the directives, saying it needed to see the FAA's final mandate.
"Some of what has to be decided is whether the responsibility lies with us -- the airlines -- or in other directions," Turk said.
Southwest and United have indicated that they do not expect the costs to be "terribly onerous," Long said.
About 2,600 737s are flown by airlines worldwide.
